editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 59 B

editorial.description: The unusually well-preserved verbatim fragments of Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, on Mind (Nous) ordering an infinity of intermingled seeds — “there is a portion of everything in everything.”

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 59 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Anaxagoras — his trial at Athens, his friendship with Pericles, and doxographical summaries of his cosmology — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 12 B

editorial.description: The six surviving fragments of Anaximander, including — via Simplicius, B1 — Western philosophy’s oldest quoted sentence: things return, by cosmic necessity, into whatever they came from, “paying penalty and retribution to one another for their injustice according to the ordering of time.”

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 12 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Anaximander of Miletus — his book, his map of the world, his astronomical models, and doxographical summaries of the apeiron doctrine — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 13 B

editorial.description: The three surviving fragments of Anaximenes, comparing the soul that holds the body together by breath to the air that encompasses and holds together the whole cosmos.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 13 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Anaximenes of Miletus — pupil of Anaximander, and doxographical summaries of his air doctrine of condensation and rarefaction — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 87 B

editorial.description: Antiphon's own words, including the long damaged papyrus fragment of On Truth (recovered from Oxyrhynchus) arguing that law is convention and nature is compulsion, alongside his On Concord, his Politicus, and the scattered word-usages later grammarians attributed to him by name.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 87 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, anecdote, and biography concerning Antiphon the sophist and dream-interpreter — including the ancient debate, preserved here directly, over whether he is the same man as Antiphon the Attic orator — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Simbeck, K. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Scripta Quae Manserunt Omnia, Fasc. 47 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1917)

editorial.description: Cato the Elder, in the last year of his long life, defends old age against the charge that it is a wretched time — arguing that it need cost no one an active, useful, or contented life.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 88 B

editorial.description: Critias' own words across every genre he wrote in: elegiac verse (a drinking-song for Sparta, a hymn to Alcibiades), the tragedies Rhadamanthys and Pirithous, the satyr-play Sisyphus (source of the boldest surviving ancient argument that the gods are a lawgiver's invention), and his prose Constitution of the Spartans.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 88 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, anecdote, and biography concerning Critias — pupil of Socrates and Gorgias, leader of the oligarchic Thirty Tyrants, and his death in the civil war that overthrew them — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Reynolds, L. D. (ed.), L. Annaei Senecae Dialogorum Libri Duodecim (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1977)

editorial.description: A defense, addressed to the young Stoic Serenus, of the paradox that the sage cannot be injured or insulted — wrongdoing may touch his body or his property, Seneca argues, but never the constancy of the wise mind itself.

editions.source: Mueller, C. F. W. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Scripta Quae Manserunt Omnia, Part 4, Vol. 2 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1890)

editorial.description: A dialogue between Cicero and his brother Quintus weighing the case for and against divination — prophecy, omens, dreams, astrology — from a broadly Academic-skeptic standpoint.

editions.source: Mueller, C. F. W. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Scripta Quae Manserunt Omnia, Part 4, Vol. 2 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1890)

editorial.description: A dialogue on fate and free will, arguing against both Stoic determinism and the Epicurean "swerve" for a middle position that preserves human responsibility — transmitted with its opening lost and a short fragment tail appended by its editors.

editions.source: Schiche, T. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Scripta Quae Manserunt Omnia, Fasc. 43 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1915)

editorial.description: A dialogue in five books surveying the rival Hellenistic accounts of the highest good — Epicurean pleasure, Stoic virtue, and the Peripatetic and Academic middle positions — through paired speeches and Cicero's own critical replies.

editions.source: de Plinval, G. (ed.), Cicéron: Traité des Lois (Paris: Les Belles Lettres, 1968)

editorial.description: A dialogue companion to the Republic, sketched in Plato's own Laws-and-Republic pairing, in which Cicero grounds Roman law in a Stoic natural-law theory and sets out a proposed law-code for the ideal state.

editions.source: Atzert, C. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Scripta Quae Manserunt Omnia, Fasc. 48 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1932)

editorial.description: Cicero's last philosophical work, a treatise on moral duty written for his son in the year before his death, drawing chiefly on the Stoic Panaetius to work out what the honorable life requires in practice.

editions.source: Reynolds, L. D. (ed.), L. Annaei Senecae Dialogorum Libri Duodecim (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1977)

editorial.description: A short dialogue answering Lucilius' question of why bad things happen to good men under a providential god — Seneca's answer: hardship is training, not punishment, and adversity is how fortune tests those it means to make strong.

editions.source: Martin, J. (ed.), T. Lucreti Cari De Rerum Natura Libri Sex (Leipzig: Teubner, 1969)

editorial.description: A six-book Latin hexameter epic expounding Epicurean physics — atoms and void, the mortal soul, and a naturalistic account of the world — composed as a cure for the fear of death and superstition.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 68 B

editorial.description: The largest surviving body of Presocratic prose — 386 fragments spanning physics, epistemology, cosmology, and (from B35 on) the ethical maxims of the "laughing philosopher," DK's Democrates gnomai on the good disposition of the soul.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 68 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Democritus of Abdera — the largest testimonia collection in the Presocratic corpus, spanning his life, his prolific writings, and doxographical summaries of atomism — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Schenkl, H. (ed.), Epicteti dissertationes ab Arriano digestae (Leipzig: Teubner, 1916, repr. 1965)

editorial.description: Arrian’s classroom transcript of his teacher’s lectures on freedom, judgement, and what is and isn’t up to us.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 31 B

editorial.description: The surviving hexameter verses of Empedocles of Acragas — On Nature, on the four roots and the cosmic cycle of Love and Strife, and the Purifications, on the soul’s exile and transmigration.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 31 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Empedocles — the original Greek text; no free English translation exists.

editions.source: Schenkl, H. (ed.), Epicteti dissertationes ab Arriano digestae (Leipzig: Teubner, 1916, repr. 1965)

editorial.description: Arrian’s pocket digest of the Discourses — Epictetus’ Stoicism boiled down to a manual for daily practice.

editions.source: Arrighetti, G. (ed.), Epicuro: Opere, 2nd ed. (Turin: Einaudi, 1973)

editorial.description: Forty numbered maxims — the "Principal Doctrines" — distilling Epicurean physics, epistemology, and ethics (including the fourfold remedy against fear of gods and death, and the account of justice as mutual advantage) into memorizable form.

editions.source: Arrighetti, G. (ed.), Epicuro: Opere, 2nd ed. (Turin: Einaudi, 1973)

editorial.description: Epicurus' summary of his physics for the beginner Herodotus — atoms and void, the infinity of worlds, and the mechanics of perception — meant to be memorized whole.

editions.source: Arrighetti, G. (ed.), Epicuro: Opere, 2nd ed. (Turin: Einaudi, 1973)

editorial.description: Epicurus' letter on ethics — pleasure as the goal, prudent reasoning about desires, and the argument that death, "the most frightening of evils," is nothing to us, since where we are, death is not, and where death is, we are not.

editions.source: Arrighetti, G. (ed.), Epicuro: Opere, 2nd ed. (Turin: Einaudi, 1973)

editorial.description: Epicurus' account of celestial and meteorological phenomena — the sun, moon, stars, storms, and comets — argued for on strictly naturalistic grounds, admitting multiple sufficient causes rather than one, so that fear of the heavens as divine agency has nothing left to attach to.

editions.source: Arrighetti, G. (ed.), Epicuro: Opere, 2nd ed. (Turin: Einaudi, 1973)

editorial.description: Eighty-one further maxims of Epicurus and his school, preserved in a single Vatican manuscript discovered in 1888 — overlapping Kuriai Doxai in places, but including sayings ("It is not the young man who should be counted happy, but the old man who has lived well") found nowhere else.

editions.source: Reynolds, L. D. (ed.), L. Annaei Senecae ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales, 2 vols. (Oxford Classical Texts, 1965)

editorial.description: One hundred and twenty-four letters of moral counsel to Lucilius, ranging freely across Stoic ethics — the fullest and most personal statement of Seneca's philosophy, each opening with its own salutation and closing with a maxim borrowed, as he says, from someone else's storeroom.

facts.author: Gorgias
facts.title: Fragments
facts.date_label: fl. c. 427 BC – d. c. 380 BC

editorial.description: Gorgias’ own words in full: the paradox-driven treatise On Not-Being, the two virtuoso display-speeches defending Helen and Palamedes, the Funeral Oration and Olympic Oration fragments, and the epigrammatic turns of phrase later critics loved to quote.

facts.author: Gorgias
facts.title: Testimonia
facts.date_label: fl. c. 427 BC – d. c. 380 BC

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 82 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, anecdote, and biography concerning Gorgias of Leontini — his embassy to Athens, his extraordinary longevity, his students (Isocrates among them), and the golden statue the Delphians raised in his own honor while he lived — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 22 B

editorial.description: The surviving quoted words of Heraclitus of Ephesus, preserved as fragments embedded in later ancient authors.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 22 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Heraclitus — the original Greek text; no free English translation exists.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 86 B

editorial.description: Hippias' own words as later sources quote them — his antiquarian Register of Olympic Victors, the bare title of his lost Trojan Dialogue, and the scattered word-usages and opinions later grammarians and mathematicians attributed to him by name.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 86 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, anecdote, and biography concerning Hippias of Elis — his feats of memory, his self-made clothes and jewelry, his lucrative embassies for his home city, and Plato's two dialogues of the same name that put his intellectual vanity on display — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Mueller, C. F. W. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Scripta Quae Manserunt Omnia, Part 4, Vol. 3 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1890)

editorial.description: Laelius, days after the sudden death of his friend Scipio Aemilianus, sets out what true friendship is and why it is possible only between good men.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 67 B

editorial.description: The three surviving fragments of Leucippus, founder of atomism — an attribution to his Great World-System, a damaged papyrus report on its disputed authorship, and the "nothing happens in vain" dictum on necessity.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 67 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Leucippus — his disputed origin and even his disputed existence, his teaching of Democritus, and doxographical summaries of the atomic theory — the original Greek text.

facts.author: Diogenes Laertius
facts.title: Lives of Eminent Philosophers
facts.latin_title: Βίοι καὶ γνῶμαι τῶν ἐν φιλοσοφίᾳ εὐδοκιμησάντων

editions.source: Long, H. S. (ed.), Diogenis Laertii Vitae philosophorum, 2 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1964, repr. 1966)

editorial.description: Ten books of biography and doxography surveying the whole of Greek philosophy, from the Seven Sages to Epicurus.

editions.source: Plasberg, O. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Academicorum Reliquiae cum Lucullo (Leipzig: Teubner, 1922)

editorial.description: The surviving half of Cicero's first edition of the Academica — Lucullus defends the possibility of certain knowledge against Cicero's own Academic-skeptic case that nothing can be known for certain.

editions.source: Farquharson, A. S. L. (ed.), The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, vol. 1 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1944, repr. 1968)

editorial.description: A Roman emperor’s private notebook of Stoic self-address, written in Greek on campaign.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 30 B

editorial.description: The surviving fragments of Melissus of Samos’ On Nature, or On What Is — the last and most systematic defense of Eleatic monism, arguing the One is infinite, motionless, and bodiless.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 30 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Melissus of Samos, admiral and philosopher — including the pseudo-Aristotelian epitome of his treatise — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Mueller, C. F. W. (ed.), M. Tulli Ciceronis Scripta Quae Manserunt Omnia, Part 4, Vol. 3 (Leipzig: Teubner, 1890)

editorial.description: Six short Stoic paradoxes — that only the honorable is good, that virtue suffices for happiness, that all wrongs are equal, that every fool is mad, that only the wise are free, and that only the wise are rich — argued in Cicero's own rhetorical voice.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 28 B

editorial.description: The surviving hexameter verses of Parmenides of Elea, preserved as quotations in later ancient authors — the goddess’s revelation of the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 28 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Parmenides — the original Greek text; no free English translation exists.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 44 B

editorial.description: The most substantial surviving Pythagorean fragments — Philolaus of Croton’s account of a cosmos fitted together out of "limiters" and "unlimiteds" bound by number and harmonia, with a central fire at the world’s hearth, the earliest Pythagorean doctrine transmitted in the philosopher’s own words.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 44 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Philolaus of Croton and Tarentum — his life among the Pythagoreans, his flight after the anti-Pythagorean uprising, and his role (per Plato’s Phaedo) as a source for Simmias and Cebes — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 84 B

editorial.description: Prodicus’ own words and Xenophon’s close paraphrase of his Heracles allegory — the choice between Virtue and Vice at the crossroads, the treatise On Nature, and the hair-splitting distinctions between near-synonyms (wish vs. desire, joy vs. pleasure) that made him famous and faintly ridiculous to his rivals.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 84 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, anecdote, and biography concerning Prodicus of Ceos — his embassies and lucrative lecture fees, his associates Theramenes and Euripides, and Socrates’ own (half-mocking) deference to his expertise in the correctness of names — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 80 B

editorial.description: Protagoras’ own words as later sources quote them — the "man is the measure" fragment, his agnostic opening on the gods, and the surviving titles of his lost treatises, including Diogenes Laertius’ own list of Protagoras’ further books.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 2 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1952), 80 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, anecdote, and biography concerning Protagoras of Abdera — his life among the sophists and Pericles’ circle, his trial and the burning of his books at Athens, and Plato’s extended portrait in the dialogue that bears his name — the original Greek text.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 14

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Pythagoras of Samos — his journeys, his teaching on the transmigration of souls, and the brotherhood he founded at Croton — the original Greek text. DK marks only one word here as Pythagoras’ own (κόσμον, “cosmos”, which he is said to have coined): he left no writings, and every other report about him is later paraphrase.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 11 B

editorial.description: Four short works or sayings attributed to Thales by later antiquity — a nautical star-guide, treatises on the solstices and equinoxes, and a summary of his water doctrine — all of doubtful or spurious authenticity, as DK itself signals and no genuine writing of Thales survives.

editions.source: Diels, H. and Kranz, W. (eds.), Die Fragmente der Vorsokratiker, 6th ed., vol. 1 (Berlin: Weidmann, 1951–52), 11 A

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Thales of Miletus — traditionally the first philosopher, credited with predicting a solar eclipse and declaring water the origin of all things — the original Greek text. DK marks no testimonium here as a verbatim quotation: Thales left no book, and every report about him is later paraphrase.

editorial.description: Five dialogues set at Cicero's Tusculan villa, arguing in turn that death is not an evil, that pain is bearable, that grief and other disturbances of the soul can be mastered by reason, and that virtue alone suffices for a happy life.

editorial.description: The surviving elegiac and hexameter verses of Xenophanes of Colophon — satires on the anthropomorphic gods of Homer and Hesiod and fragments of a single, motionless god unlike mortals in form or thought.

editorial.description: Ancient reports, paraphrases, and biography concerning Xenophanes — the original Greek text; no free English translation exists.

editorial.description: The four surviving fragments of Zeno of Elea, defending Parmenides’ One against plurality — the seeds of his famous paradoxes of motion.
